description:
Hi! I’m Oscar, a 3D artist and game developer from Barcelona. I’ve shipped multiplayer indie games, so I’m used to turning ideas into polished, playable prototypes fast.

I bring 3D art, real-time visuals and interactive design, and I’d love to work on a challenge where visualization or gamification helps people explore space and Earth data.

Looking for teammates with skills in data science, web/backend development, science or engineering, and pitching/storytelling. Let’s build something cool!
summary:
LULA Navigator is a free, offline 3D web app that shows where the Sun and Earth sit in the sky at any lunar landing site, on any date from 2020 to 2040, and how long remains before sunset or Earthset.

The challenge names the gap: the data exists in QuickMap, Moon Trek and JPL Horizons, but those interfaces are built for specialists and slow to compare. LULA Navigator collapses the question to one screen. Pick a site — Shackleton rim, Malapert, Apollo 11, a CLPS target, or your own coordinates — and a date, and the app puts the Sun and Earth against the real LOLA terrain horizon.

The orbit view shows the Moon, with the Sun and Earth behind it in their true directions. The surface view stands you on the site. A timeline scrubs a lunar month and reports sunlight percentage, Earth-link percentage, longest darkness and longest communication gap, ending in a plain-language landing verdict.
details:
What it does

LULA Navigator answers one operational question — can this lander see the Sun and Earth from this spot, at this time, and for how long — in three linked views. The orbit view shows the Moon with real relief, the Sun and Earth behind it in their true directions, Earth at true size and distance; click the Moon to set a site. The surface view puts the camera 2 m above that site, with real terrain out to 220 km on the curved Moon; the Sun and Earth are drawn at true angular size and disappear behind the terrain exactly when the computed horizon says so. A timeline and horizon panorama scrub a lunar month, reporting elevation, time to sunset or Earthset, sunlight %, Earth-in-view %, longest darkness and longest communication gap. A rating panel turns this into a plain-language verdict on power, Earth link and slope, with gates: no Sun at landing means not viable, not a misleading score.

How it works

JPL Horizons (DE441) supplies a two-hour table of sub-solar and sub-Earth points, distances and lunar orientation. The browser interpolates it into azimuth and elevation in the site's local frame, on a spherical Moon (R = 1737.4 km) with no refraction. The horizon comes from LRO LOLA elevation in 0.5° bins out to 220 km, curvature included, from an eye 2 m up. A body is visible while any part of its disc clears that horizon; rise and set are bisected to 15 seconds. Checked against Horizons at 345 epochs between 2024 and 2035: worst error 0.0002° for the Sun, 0.0061° for Earth.

Benefits and impact

A launch delay now takes two clicks instead of a manual re-check, and every scenario is a URL you can send to a colleague. A planner sees in seconds that moving 300 m along the Shackleton rim cuts yearly sunlight from 96% to 69%. The same screen works in a classroom: the verdict is plain language and the extreme geometry is shown, not asserted.

Tools

TypeScript, React, three.js and React Three Fiber, Vite and Tailwind CSS. Node scripts query Horizons and validate the maths; Python (NumPy, Pillow, OpenEXR) builds the terrain pipeline. Docker serves the static site — no backend, no account. All data is NASA (JPL Horizons, LRO LOLA, LROC WAC, Blue Marble, NASA star maps), about 96 MB bundled, so it runs offline.

Creativity

The interface is the physics: bodies at true angular size, occluded by real terrain, so a user reads the sky the way the solar array and antenna would, instead of decoding a chart.

What the team considered

Accuracy against browser weight: a 220 km horizon in 0.5° bins, with terrain precomputed offline. Accessibility: colour is never the only signal, and verdicts are written for non-specialists. Honesty: grid resolution (about 475 m at the pole), no Earth-eclipse modelling, no guesses for boulders, thermal, radiation or science value. No AI model generates or alters any value shown.
